lessons.title: Machine learning fundamentals: learning types, data splits and generalisation
lessons.summary: Supervised versus unsupervised learning, feature engineering, train/validation/test splits, cross-validation, and the bias-variance trade-off behind overfitting and underfitting.

sections.heading: Kinds of learning
sections.body:
- **Supervised learning** trains on labelled examples (input → known output). **Classification** predicts a category (spam / not spam); **regression** predicts a number (a price, a temperature).
- **Unsupervised learning** finds structure in unlabelled data: **clustering** (for example k-means for customer segments), **dimensionality reduction** (for example PCA for visualisation), anomaly detection.
- **Self-supervised learning** creates labels from the data itself. LLM pre-training is self-supervised: the "label" for each position is simply the next token (or a masked token) in the text.
- **Reinforcement learning** learns from a reward signal rather than fixed labels. It shows up in LLMs as the RL step of RLHF.

Exam questions often describe a business need and ask which kind of learning fits. The tell is the data: labels present → supervised; no labels and you want groups → clustering.

sections.heading: Features and feature engineering
Train, validation and test
sections.body:
- **Training set:** the data the model's weights are fitted on.
- **Validation set:** data used to choose hyperparameters, compare models and decide when to stop training.
- **Test set:** held back until the end for a single, unbiased estimate of performance on new data.

If you tune repeatedly against the test set, information leaks into your choices and the test score becomes optimistic. **k-fold cross-validation** splits the data into k folds, trains k times holding out a different fold each time, and averages the scores. It gives a steadier estimate when data is limited and is a standard way to **compare models** fairly.

sections.heading: Overfitting, underfitting and the bias-variance trade-off
sections.body:
- **Underfitting (high bias):** the model is too simple. Training and validation error are **both** high. Fix with more capacity, better features or longer training.
- **Overfitting (high variance):** the model memorises the training data. Training error is low but validation error is much higher. Fix with more (or augmented) data, **regularisation** (L1/L2 weight penalties, also called weight decay), **dropout**, **early stopping**, or a smaller model.

The NVIDIA DLI *Fundamentals of Deep Learning* course demonstrates this directly: a model that scores almost perfectly on training images but poorly on validation images is overfitting, and **data augmentation** (random flips, rotations, zooms) improves generalisation by showing the model more varied examples.

keyPoints: Labels present → supervised (classification or regression); no labels → unsupervised (clustering, dimensionality reduction).
LLM pre-training is self-supervised: the next token is the label.
Validation data chooses hyperparameters; the test set is used once at the end.
k-fold cross-validation gives a more reliable comparison when data is limited.
High train and validation error = underfitting; low train but high validation error = overfitting.
Regularisation, dropout, early stopping and data augmentation all fight overfitting.

gotchas.trap: Tuning hyperparameters against the test set because it is "the most honest number".
gotchas.correct: Tune on a validation set (or with cross-validation) and touch the test set once; otherwise the test score is optimistically biased.

gotchas.trap: Training longer to fix a large gap between training and validation accuracy.
gotchas.correct: A large gap means overfitting; more epochs usually widen it. Use regularisation, augmentation, more data or early stopping.

gotchas.trap: Calling LLM pre-training "unsupervised, so it has no labels at all".
gotchas.correct: It is self-supervised: the targets (next or masked tokens) come from the text itself.

lessons.lab: Open the NVDLI Fundamentals of Deep Learning notebooks and train the ASL image classifier. Plot training versus validation accuracy, note the overfitting gap, then add data augmentation and compare the curves.

lessons.title: Neural networks: activations, loss functions and gradient descent
lessons.summary: How a neural network learns: neurons and layers, activation functions, matching losses to tasks, backpropagation, learning rate, optimisers and transfer learning.

sections.heading: Neurons, layers and activations
sections.body:
A neuron computes a weighted sum of its inputs plus a bias, then applies a non-linear **activation function**. Stacking layers of neurons lets the network model complex functions; without non-linear activations, any stack of layers collapses into a single linear transformation.

| Activation | Shape | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| **ReLU** | max(0, x) | Default for hidden layers; cheap and reduces vanishing gradients |
| **Sigmoid** | squashes to (0, 1) | Binary classification output; probability of one class |
| **Tanh** | squashes to (−1, 1) | Older recurrent networks |
| **Softmax** | turns a vector into probabilities summing to 1 | Multi-class output layer; also inside attention |
| **GELU** | smooth ReLU-like curve | Common in Transformer feed-forward layers |

Sigmoid and tanh **saturate**: for large inputs their gradient is close to zero, which causes **vanishing gradients** in deep networks. That is a main reason ReLU-family activations replaced them in hidden layers.

sections.heading: Loss functions
sections.body:
The **loss** measures how wrong the predictions are; training minimises it.
- **Mean squared error (MSE)** for regression.
- **Binary cross-entropy** for two-class problems with a sigmoid output.
- **Categorical cross-entropy** for multi-class problems with a softmax output. LLMs are trained with cross-entropy over the vocabulary at each position, and **perplexity** is the exponential of that average loss.

Choose the loss that matches the output: a softmax layer paired with MSE trains poorly compared with cross-entropy.

sections.heading: Gradient descent and backpropagation
sections.body:
**Backpropagation** applies the chain rule to compute the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight. **Gradient descent** then moves each weight a small step against its gradient. The size of that step is the **learning rate**:
- too high → the loss oscillates or diverges (can become NaN);
- too low → training is very slow or stalls.

Variants: **batch** gradient descent uses all data per step, **stochastic** uses one example, and **mini-batch** (the norm) uses a small batch, which fits GPU parallelism. One **epoch** is a full pass over the training data. Adaptive optimisers such as **Adam** keep per-parameter estimates of the gradient's first and second moments and adjust step sizes automatically; Adam (and its weight-decay variant AdamW) is the usual choice for Transformers.

sections.heading: Transfer learning
sections.body: Training a large network from scratch needs lots of data and compute. **Transfer learning** starts from a model pretrained on a large dataset, **freezes** most of its layers, replaces the final layer with a new head for your task, and trains only the new parts. Once the head converges you can optionally **fine-tune** by unfreezing some layers with a low learning rate. The DLI course uses exactly this pattern with a pretrained image model, and the same idea, at much larger scale, underlies fine-tuning a pretrained LLM.

keyPoints: Non-linear activations are what make depth useful; ReLU is the default hidden activation.
Softmax + categorical cross-entropy for multi-class; sigmoid + binary cross-entropy for binary; MSE for regression.
Saturating activations (sigmoid, tanh) cause vanishing gradients in deep networks.
Diverging or oscillating loss usually means the learning rate is too high.
Adam/AdamW adapt per-parameter step sizes and are standard for Transformers.
Transfer learning: freeze the pretrained base, train a new head, then optionally fine-tune with a low learning rate.

gotchas.trap: Using softmax on hidden layers to "normalise" activations.
gotchas.correct: Softmax belongs on a multi-class output (and inside attention). Hidden layers use ReLU/GELU-style activations.

gotchas.trap: Assuming a lower loss on training data always means a better model.
gotchas.correct: Judge on validation loss; training loss can keep falling while the model overfits.

gotchas.trap: Fine-tuning a whole pretrained network with a high learning rate on a tiny dataset.
gotchas.correct: Freeze the base first and use a low learning rate when unfreezing, or the pretrained features get destroyed.

lessons.lab: In the NVDLI notebooks, retrain the pretrained-model exercise twice: once with the base frozen and once fully unfrozen at a high learning rate. Compare validation accuracy and explain the difference.

lessons.title: Transformer architecture: tokens, embeddings and self-attention
lessons.summary: How Transformers turn text into tokens and vectors, how scaled dot-product and multi-head attention work, why positional information is needed, and how encoder, decoder and decoder-only models differ.

sections.heading: Tokenisation
sections.body:
Models read **tokens**, not words. Modern LLMs use **subword** tokenisers such as byte-pair encoding (BPE), which start from characters (or bytes) and merge frequent pairs into larger units. Common words become one token; rare words, names and code split into several pieces, so there is no true "out-of-vocabulary" word.

Consequences you will be tested on:
- **Context limits, throughput and usually pricing are measured in tokens**, not words or characters.
- The same text can produce different token counts with different tokenisers; non-English text and code often need more tokens per word.
- A model must be used with the tokeniser it was trained with.

sections.heading: Embeddings
sections.body:
Each token ID is mapped to a dense **embedding vector** learned during training. Vectors for related meanings end up close together in that space (word2vec showed this with simple models). Inside a Transformer, embeddings become **contextual**: after attention layers, the vector for "bank" differs in "river bank" and "bank loan".

Separate **text-embedding models** produce one vector per sentence or passage. Comparing those vectors with **cosine similarity** powers semantic search, clustering and the retrieval step of RAG.

sections.heading: Self-attention
sections.body:
For each token, the model computes a **query (Q)**, a **key (K)** and a **value (V)** vector. Attention scores are dot products of a token's query with every key, scaled by **1/√d_k** and passed through **softmax**; the output is the weighted sum of the values:

`Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(QKᵀ / √d_k) V`

The paper scales by √d_k because large dot products push softmax into regions with extremely small gradients. **Multi-head attention** runs several attention operations in parallel on different learned projections so the model can "jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions", then concatenates the results.

Because every token attends to every other token in one step, the Transformer drops recurrence entirely. That makes training **highly parallel** on GPUs, but attention cost grows **quadratically** with sequence length, which is one reason context windows are finite.

sections.heading: Positional information
sections.body: Self-attention by itself has no notion of order: shuffle the tokens and each one sees the same set of keys. The original Transformer adds **positional encodings** (fixed sine and cosine functions of position) to the input embeddings; later models use learned position embeddings or rotary/relative schemes. The goal is the same: inject the order of the sequence.

sections.heading: Encoder, decoder and decoder-only
sections.body:
| Architecture | Attention | Typical pre-training | Good for | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Encoder-only** | Bidirectional (sees left and right) | Masked language modelling | Classification, NER, embeddings, extractive tasks | BERT |
| **Encoder-decoder** | Encoder bidirectional; decoder causal plus cross-attention to encoder | Sequence-to-sequence | Translation, summarisation | Original Transformer, T5 |
| **Decoder-only** | **Causal** (masked): each token sees only earlier tokens | Next-token prediction | Open-ended generation, chat | GPT-style LLMs |

The **context window** is the maximum number of tokens (prompt plus generated output) a model can attend to at once. Anything beyond it is invisible to the model, so long documents must be chunked, summarised or retrieved selectively.

keyPoints: Subword tokenisation (BPE) means rare words split into pieces; limits and costs are counted in tokens.
Embeddings place similar meanings near each other; cosine similarity compares them.
Attention = softmax(QKᵀ/√d_k)V; the √d_k scaling keeps softmax gradients usable.
Multi-head attention attends to different representation subspaces in parallel.
Positional encodings are needed because attention is order-agnostic.
Encoder-only (BERT) for understanding; encoder-decoder for seq2seq; decoder-only with causal masking for generation.
Attention cost grows quadratically with sequence length, so context windows are finite.

gotchas.trap: Assuming a context limit is a word count.
gotchas.correct: It is a token count, and it covers the prompt plus the generated output.

gotchas.trap: Choosing a decoder-only chat model as the default for every NLP task.
gotchas.correct: For classification, NER or embeddings, an encoder-only model like BERT is often smaller, faster and fits better.

gotchas.trap: Believing Transformers process tokens one by one like RNNs during training.
gotchas.correct: Training processes all positions in parallel; only generation is token-by-token (autoregressive).

lessons.lab: Read Sections 3.2 to 3.5 of "Attention Is All You Need". On paper, compute single-head attention for a three-token sequence with 2-dimensional Q, K and V, including the √d_k scaling and softmax, and apply a causal mask to see how the output changes.

lessons.title: The LLM lifecycle: pre-training, instruction tuning and alignment
lessons.summary: How a base model is pre-trained, why instruction tuning turns it into an assistant, and how RLHF and preference methods align it with human intent.

sections.heading: Pre-training
sections.body:
Pre-training learns general language ability from a very large unlabelled corpus with a self-supervised objective:
- **Causal language modelling** (decoder-only, GPT style): predict the next token from everything before it.
- **Masked language modelling** (encoder-only, BERT style): hide about 15% of tokens and predict them from both sides. BERT also used a **next sentence prediction** task.

The result is a **base (foundation) model**. It is a strong text continuer but not an assistant: ask it a question and it may continue with more questions. Pre-training is by far the most compute-intensive stage, which is why most teams start from an existing foundation model instead of training one.

sections.heading: Supervised fine-tuning and instruction tuning
sections.body:
**Supervised fine-tuning (SFT)** continues training on labelled examples. **Instruction tuning** is SFT on many tasks phrased as natural-language instructions with good responses. The FLAN work showed that instruction tuning a pretrained model across many tasks substantially improves its **zero-shot** performance on unseen tasks. Instruction-tuned ("instruct" or "chat") models follow requests instead of merely continuing text.

Full fine-tuning updates every weight, which is expensive and risks **catastrophic forgetting** of general skills. Parameter-efficient methods (next lesson) are the common alternative.

sections.heading: RLHF
sections.body:
**Reinforcement learning from human feedback** aligns a model with what people actually prefer (helpful, honest, harmless). The InstructGPT recipe has three steps:
1. **SFT** on human-written demonstrations of the desired behaviour.
2. **Reward model:** humans rank several model outputs for the same prompt; a model is trained to predict those preferences as a scalar reward.
3. **RL optimisation:** the policy (the LLM) is optimised against the reward model with **PPO**, with a penalty that keeps it close to the SFT model so it does not drift or "game" the reward.

InstructGPT found that labelers preferred outputs from a 1.3B-parameter RLHF model over the 175B GPT-3 base model, showing that alignment is not just about size. Collecting human preference rankings is therefore a real job in LLM projects, and the NCA-GENL subtopics mention taking part in it.

sections.heading: Preference optimisation without RL
sections.body: **Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)** trains directly on preference pairs (chosen versus rejected responses) with a simple classification-style loss, avoiding a separate reward model and the RL loop. It is a popular, simpler alternative to PPO-based RLHF that uses the same kind of human preference data.

keyPoints: Pre-training is self-supervised: next-token (causal) or masked-token (MLM) prediction.
A base model continues text; instruction tuning makes it follow instructions and improves zero-shot behaviour.
RLHF = SFT → reward model trained on human rankings → PPO against the reward model with a KL penalty.
DPO uses the same preference data without a separate reward model or RL loop.
Full fine-tuning is costly and risks catastrophic forgetting.

gotchas.trap: Thinking RLHF trains the LLM directly on human ratings in one step.
gotchas.correct: Human rankings train a reward model first; the LLM is then optimised against that reward model.

gotchas.trap: Deploying a base model as a chatbot and expecting instruction following.
gotchas.correct: Use an instruction-tuned or chat-aligned model; base models just continue text.

gotchas.trap: Assuming the biggest model always gives the most preferred answers.
gotchas.correct: InstructGPT showed a much smaller aligned model was preferred over a far larger base model.

lessons.lab: Write five prompts and send each to a base model and an instruct model of the same family (for example via the NVIDIA API catalog). Rank the paired outputs yourself as a labeler would, and note which behaviours instruction tuning and alignment changed.

lessons.title: Customising LLMs: prompt engineering, p-tuning and LoRA
lessons.summary: The cheapest-first ladder for adapting an LLM: zero-shot, few-shot and chain-of-thought prompting, then parameter-efficient fine-tuning with p-tuning, prompt tuning and LoRA.

sections.heading: Prompt engineering
sections.body:
Prompt engineering changes the input, not the weights, so it is the fastest and cheapest thing to try first.
- **Zero-shot:** give only the instruction ("Classify this review as positive or negative").
- **Few-shot (in-context learning):** include a handful of input → output examples in the prompt. GPT-3 showed large models can pick up a task from such demonstrations without any gradient updates. Few-shot examples are especially good for enforcing an **output format**.
- **Chain-of-thought (CoT):** show or request intermediate reasoning steps before the final answer. CoT prompting markedly improves multi-step arithmetic, commonsense and symbolic reasoning in sufficiently large models.
- Good practice: clear instructions, a role or persona, explicit constraints, delimiters around supplied content, and a specified output schema.

Limits: prompts consume context tokens on every call, and some behaviours (domain style, specialised tasks at scale) cannot be reached by prompting alone.

sections.heading: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT)
sections.body:
PEFT adapts a model by training a small number of new parameters while the pretrained weights stay **frozen**. It needs far less GPU memory and storage than full fine-tuning and reduces catastrophic forgetting.

**P-tuning and prompt tuning.** Instead of hand-writing a text prompt, the model learns **continuous "virtual token" embeddings** that are prepended to the input. In p-tuning, a small trainable **prompt encoder** (an LSTM plus MLP in the original p-tuning paper) generates these virtual tokens; in the narrower sense, prompt tuning learns the embeddings directly (NVIDIA's blog uses the two names almost interchangeably). After tuning, NVIDIA's blog explains, the virtual tokens are stored in a lookup table for inference, and models p-tuned on different tasks can be saved without large amounts of memory, so one frozen base model can serve many tasks.

**LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation).** LoRA freezes the pretrained weights and injects **trainable low-rank decomposition matrices** (W + BA, with rank r much smaller than the layer size) into Transformer layers, typically the attention projections. The paper reports cutting trainable parameters by about 10,000× and GPU memory by about 3× for GPT-3 175B versus full fine-tuning, with **no additional inference latency** because the low-rank update can be merged into the base weights. Small per-task adapters can be stored and swapped on one shared base model.

sections.heading: Choosing an approach
sections.body:
| Need | First choice |
|---|---|
| Quick improvement, consistent format | Prompting (zero/few-shot) |
| Multi-step reasoning | Chain-of-thought prompting |
| Up-to-date or private facts, citations | RAG (next lesson) |
| Domain style or a specialised task across many calls | PEFT (LoRA, p-tuning) |
| Deep behaviour change with lots of data and compute | Full fine-tuning |

Fine-tuning teaches **behaviour and style** well but is a poor way to inject frequently changing **facts**; that is what retrieval is for.

keyPoints: Try prompting first: zero-shot, then few-shot, then chain-of-thought for reasoning.
Few-shot examples are in-context learning: no weights change.
P-tuning/prompt tuning learn virtual token embeddings; p-tuning uses a small prompt encoder; the LLM stays frozen.
LoRA trains low-rank matrices beside frozen weights; adapters are tiny and can be merged for no extra inference latency.
PEFT saves memory and storage and lets one base model serve many tasks.
Use RAG, not fine-tuning, for knowledge that changes often.

gotchas.trap: Saying few-shot prompting "fine-tunes" the model.
gotchas.correct: Few-shot examples live only in the prompt; no parameters are updated.

gotchas.trap: Assuming LoRA always slows inference because it adds layers.
gotchas.correct: The low-rank update can be merged into the base weights, so LoRA adds no inference latency.

gotchas.trap: Fine-tuning a model every week to keep it current with new documents.
gotchas.correct: Retrieval-augmented generation keeps answers current without retraining.

lessons.lab: Take a small classification task and measure accuracy with a zero-shot prompt, a five-shot prompt, and a chain-of-thought prompt. Then read Section 4 of the LoRA paper and write down which weight matrices are adapted and why the method adds no inference latency.

lessons.title: RAG, embeddings and decoding strategies
lessons.summary: How retrieval-augmented generation grounds an LLM in your data, the role of embedding and reranking models and vector databases, and how temperature, top-k and top-p shape generated text.

sections.heading: Why RAG
sections.body: LLMs only know what was in their training data, up to a cutoff, and they can **hallucinate** plausible but wrong answers. **Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)** fetches relevant passages from an external knowledge source at query time and adds them to the prompt so the model answers from that evidence. NVIDIA's explainer highlights the benefits: answers grounded in current or private data, **citations** users can check, fewer hallucinations, and no need to retrain the model when the data changes.

sections.heading: The RAG pipeline
sections.body:
**Ingestion (offline):**
1. Load documents and split them into **chunks** (sized to fit the context and keep one idea per chunk, often with some overlap).
2. Convert each chunk to a vector with an **embedding model**.
3. Store vectors plus metadata in a **vector database** (Milvus is the one on NVIDIA's reading list) with an index for fast approximate nearest-neighbour search.

**Query time (online):**
1. Embed the user question with the **same** embedding model.
2. Retrieve the top-k most similar chunks (cosine or dot-product similarity), optionally combined with keyword search.
3. Optionally **rerank** candidates with a cross-encoder reranking model for higher precision.
4. Insert the best chunks into the prompt and let the LLM generate a grounded answer with citations.

NVIDIA packages embedding and reranking models as **NeMo Retriever** NIM microservices (text embedding and text reranking), alongside LLM NIMs for generation.

sections.heading: Common RAG failure points
sections.body:
- **Irrelevant retrieval:** poor chunking, a mismatched embedding model, or no reranking. Fix retrieval before blaming the LLM.
- **Query and document embedded with different models:** the vectors are not comparable.
- **Too many chunks stuffed into the prompt:** higher cost and latency, and the relevant passage can be buried.
- **Stale index:** re-embed and re-index documents when they change.

sections.heading: Decoding: how tokens are chosen
sections.body:
At each step the model outputs a probability distribution over the vocabulary. The **decoding strategy** picks the next token:
- **Greedy:** always the most likely token. Deterministic but can be repetitive.
- **Beam search:** keeps several candidate sequences; common in translation.
- **Temperature:** divides the logits before softmax. **Low (near 0)** sharpens the distribution → focused, near-deterministic output (good for extraction, code, factual QA). **High** flattens it → more diverse and creative but more error-prone.
- **Top-k:** sample only from the k most likely tokens. **k = 1 is greedy.**
- **Top-p (nucleus):** sample from the **smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability reaches p**. The set adapts: small when the model is confident, larger when it is not. The nucleus-sampling paper introduced it to avoid both the bland repetition of greedy/beam decoding and the incoherent tail of pure sampling.

Other controls include maximum new tokens, stop sequences, and repetition or frequency penalties.

keyPoints: RAG grounds answers in retrieved, current or private data and enables citations without retraining.
Pipeline: chunk → embed → vector DB → retrieve top-k → (rerank) → prompt the LLM.
Query and documents must use the same embedding model.
NeMo Retriever NIMs provide embedding and reranking models.
Low temperature = focused and repeatable; high temperature = diverse and riskier.
Top-k keeps a fixed number of candidates (k = 1 is greedy); top-p keeps the smallest set reaching cumulative probability p.

gotchas.trap: Raising temperature to fix wrong facts in a RAG app.
gotchas.correct: Wrong facts usually come from retrieval; fix chunking, embeddings or reranking. Lower temperature for factual tasks.

gotchas.trap: Thinking top-p keeps a fixed number of tokens.
gotchas.correct: That is top-k. Top-p keeps however many tokens are needed to reach cumulative probability p.

gotchas.trap: Stuffing as many retrieved chunks as fit into the context.
gotchas.correct: Retrieve and rerank for precision; extra chunks add cost and can bury the relevant passage.

lessons.lab: Build a minimal RAG notebook: chunk a few internal-style documents, embed them with an embedding model from the NVIDIA API catalog, retrieve with cosine similarity, and answer questions with an LLM. Then run the same question at temperature 0 and 1.0, and at top-p 0.5 and 0.95, and compare the outputs.

lessons.title: Curating LLM training data with NeMo Curator
lessons.summary: How raw text becomes training-ready data: cleaning, language ID, heuristic and classifier filtering, three kinds of deduplication, tokenization and synthetic data, using NVIDIA NeMo Curator as the reference tool.

sections.heading: Why curation matters
sections.body:
Model quality depends heavily on data quality. Web-scale text is full of boilerplate, near-copies, other languages, spam and unsafe content. Training on it wastes GPU hours, and the model can memorise repeated passages. The exam's official subtopics include preparing large datasets (scraping, tokenization) for pretraining, fine-tuning and RLHF. Curation is the step that makes those datasets usable.

A typical text pipeline runs in this order:

1. **Extract and clean**: strip HTML, fix Unicode and normalise whitespace.
2. **Identify language**: keep only the target languages.
3. **Filter**: apply cheap heuristic rules first, then ML quality, domain and safety classifiers.
4. **Deduplicate**: exact, then fuzzy, then semantic.
5. **Redact or flag sensitive content** where needed (PII), then **tokenize** and shard.

Run the cheap steps first so the expensive GPU steps see less data.

sections.heading: NeMo Curator at a glance
sections.body:
**NeMo Curator** is NVIDIA's open-source, scalable data-curation library. It now covers **text, image, video and audio**.

- **Language identification**: FastText and GlotLID models.
- **Heuristic filters**: rule-based checks such as document length, symbol-to-word ratio, repeated lines or n-grams, and URL density.
- **Classifier filters**: quality, domain and safety classifiers. These include lightweight FastText classifiers and GPU-distributed model-based classifiers.
- **Synthetic data**: LLM-based generation of new examples, for instance to fill gaps in a fine-tuning set.
- **Scaling**: the execution backend **moved from Dask to Ray** (Ray Data, Xenna and Ray Actor Pool executors), and the docs include a migration guide. Older tutorials that show Dask clusters describe the previous design.

The NVIDIA Trust Center still uses the older name "NeMo Data Curator".

sections.heading: Three kinds of deduplication
sections.body:
| Type | How it works | Catches |
|---|---|---|
| **Exact** | Hash each document (MD5) and drop identical hashes | Byte-identical copies |
| **Fuzzy** | **MinHash** signatures plus **locality-sensitive hashing (LSH)** to bucket similar documents; GPU-accelerated | Near-duplicates: same article with a different header, date or footer |
| **Semantic** | Embed documents, **cluster** the embeddings and drop items that are too close within a cluster | Paraphrases and different wording of the same content |

Exact dedup is cheapest but misses almost-identical pages. Fuzzy dedup handles template noise. Semantic dedup is the most expensive and the only one of the three that catches meaning-level redundancy.

sections.heading: Tokenization and the final dataset
sections.body:
Models consume **tokens**, not characters. Subword tokenizers (for example BERT's **WordPiece**, or BPE in many decoder models) split rare words into pieces so the vocabulary stays fixed in size. Practical consequences:

- Always tokenize with the **same tokenizer as the model** you will train or fine-tune. Token IDs are not portable between vocabularies.
- Measure dataset size and sequence lengths **in tokens**. Context limits and training cost are counted in tokens.
- Check the **token-length distribution** (a histogram) before choosing a maximum sequence length, so you know how much truncation or padding you cause.

For fine-tuning and RLHF, the "dataset" is often prompt–response pairs or preference pairs (chosen vs rejected). The same rules apply: dedupe, filter for quality and safety, and hold out an evaluation split that does not overlap with training data.

keyPoints: Order the pipeline cheap to expensive: clean, language ID, heuristic filters, classifiers, then dedup.
Exact dedup = hashing; fuzzy = MinHash + LSH; semantic = embeddings + clustering.
NeMo Curator is open source, multimodal, and now runs on a Ray backend (previously Dask).
Tokenize with the target model's tokenizer and size everything in tokens.
Synthetic data from an LLM can fill coverage gaps but still needs filtering and dedup.

gotchas.trap: Exact hashing removes near-duplicate web pages.
gotchas.correct: Exact hashing only removes identical documents. Near-duplicates need fuzzy (MinHash + LSH) dedup, and paraphrases need semantic dedup.

gotchas.trap: NeMo Curator scales with Dask.
gotchas.correct: The current NeMo Curator backend is Ray. Dask was the earlier design.

gotchas.trap: Any tokenizer works as long as the vocabulary is large.
gotchas.correct: Token IDs only make sense for the tokenizer the model was trained with. Use the model's own tokenizer.

lessons.lab: Take 200 short documents (for example scraped product descriptions). Compute an MD5 hash per document and count exact duplicates. Then normalise case and whitespace and hash again, and note how many more duplicates appear. Finally list three near-duplicate pairs that hashing still misses; these are what MinHash + LSH would catch.

lessons.title: GPU-accelerated data science with RAPIDS cuDF and cuML
lessons.summary: Speeding up exploratory analysis and classical ML on GPUs with cuDF, cudf.pandas, cuML and cuml.accel, and knowing when acceleration applies.

sections.heading: RAPIDS, now NVIDIA CUDA-X Data Science
sections.body:
**RAPIDS** is NVIDIA's suite of GPU data-science libraries. NVIDIA now brands it as **CUDA-X libraries for data science**, and the docs moved from docs.rapids.ai to docs.nvidia.com/datascience. The library names are unchanged:

- **cuDF**: a GPU DataFrame library with a **pandas-like API**, built on the C++ library libcudf.
- **cuML**: GPU-accelerated machine-learning algorithms with an API that mirrors **scikit-learn** (fit / predict / transform).

Both are on the exam's official reading list, alongside NVIDIA's GPU data-science blog.

sections.heading: cuDF and cudf.pandas
sections.body:
You can use cuDF in two ways:

1. **Directly**: `import cudf` and work with `cudf.DataFrame`. Most of the API matches pandas.
2. **cudf.pandas (zero code change)**: keep your pandas code and turn on the accelerator:
   - in Jupyter: `%load_ext cudf.pandas` before importing pandas
   - for a script: `python -m cudf.pandas script.py`
   - in code: `cudf.pandas.install()`

With cudf.pandas, supported operations run on the GPU. Anything unsupported **falls back to regular pandas on the CPU** automatically, so the code still runs correctly. Heavy fallback reduces the speedup, so profile if a workload is slower than expected.

cuDF also provides a GPU engine for **Polars** users.

sections.heading: cuML and cuml.accel
sections.body:
cuML offers 50+ algorithms: regression, classification, clustering (for example k-means, DBSCAN), dimensionality reduction (PCA, UMAP, t-SNE) and nearest neighbours. NVIDIA's docs cite an **average speedup of 10–50x** over CPU equivalents. Treat that as a typical range, not a guarantee; small datasets may see little gain because of data-transfer and launch overhead.

- **cuml.accel** accelerates existing scikit-learn code with zero code changes, in the same spirit as cudf.pandas.
- **Scaling out**: cuML scales to multiple GPUs and nodes through **Dask**.

A common LLM-adjacent use is reducing **embedding vectors** to 2-D with GPU UMAP or t-SNE, then plotting them to inspect clusters, outliers and near-duplicates.

sections.heading: When the GPU helps
sections.body:
GPU acceleration pays off when:

- data is large (millions of rows) and operations are vectorised (joins, group-bys, sorts, string operations)
- you iterate many times, as in exploratory analysis or hyperparameter sweeps

It helps less when:

- data is tiny, so transfer overhead dominates
- code relies on row-by-row Python loops or `apply` with arbitrary Python functions, which defeat vectorisation
- the data does not fit in GPU memory (then use chunking, multi-GPU via Dask, or a larger GPU)

Results should match the CPU libraries closely. Small floating-point differences between CPU and GPU implementations are normal, so compare metrics with a tolerance rather than exact equality.

keyPoints: cuDF ≈ pandas on GPU; cuML ≈ scikit-learn on GPU.
cudf.pandas and cuml.accel give zero-code-change acceleration with automatic CPU fallback for cudf.pandas.
Enable cudf.pandas with %load_ext cudf.pandas, python -m cudf.pandas, or cudf.pandas.install().
cuML scales multi-GPU / multi-node via Dask.
RAPIDS is now branded NVIDIA CUDA-X Data Science; library names are unchanged.

gotchas.trap: cudf.pandas raises an error when it meets an unsupported pandas operation.
gotchas.correct: It falls back to pandas on the CPU for that operation and keeps running.

gotchas.trap: Moving any workload to cuDF always makes it 10–50x faster.
gotchas.correct: Speedups depend on data size and operation type. Small data and Python-level loops see little or no gain.

gotchas.trap: Using cuML means rewriting models in a new API.
gotchas.correct: cuML mirrors the scikit-learn estimator API, and cuml.accel can accelerate unchanged scikit-learn code.

lessons.lab: Load a CSV of at least a few million rows with pandas and time a group-by and a join. Restart the kernel, run %load_ext cudf.pandas before importing pandas, and rerun the same cells unchanged. Record both timings and note any operation that ran noticeably slower, which hints at CPU fallback.

lessons.title: Analysing results: charts, statistical metrics and trends
lessons.summary: Choosing the right chart, comparing models with loss, R² and explained variance, and spotting trends and confounders that could mislead an analysis.

sections.heading: Pick the chart for the question
sections.body:
The official Data Analysis subtopics include data mining and visualisation and creating graphs and charts with specialised software (the reading list names Matplotlib and the Python Data Science Handbook).

| Question | Chart |
|---|---|
| How is one variable distributed (token lengths, latency)? | **Histogram** or box plot |
| How do two numeric variables relate? | **Scatter plot** |
| How does a value change over steps or time (training loss)? | **Line chart** |
| How do categories compare (error rate per language)? | **Bar chart** |
| Where do embeddings cluster? | 2-D **scatter** after PCA/UMAP/t-SNE |
| Which predictions get confused? | **Confusion matrix** heatmap |

Label axes and units, start bar-chart axes at zero, and use a log scale when values span orders of magnitude.

sections.heading: Comparing models with statistical metrics
sections.body:
**Loss** is what training minimises: cross-entropy for classification and next-token prediction, mean squared error (MSE) for regression. Plot **training and validation loss** together:

- both falling: still learning
- training falls while validation rises: **overfitting**; consider early stopping, regularisation or more data
- both high and flat: **underfitting**; consider a larger model, better features or more training

For regression, two variance-based metrics appear often:

- **R² (coefficient of determination)** = 1 − SS_res / SS_tot. 1.0 is perfect, 0 matches always predicting the mean, and it can be negative for a model worse than the mean.
- **Explained variance** = 1 − Var(y − ŷ) / Var(y). It ignores a constant offset in the errors, so a model that is consistently biased can score high on explained variance yet lower on R². The two are identical when residuals have zero mean, and the scikit-learn guide recommends R² in general for this reason.

Compare models on the **same held-out data**, and prefer cross-validation when data is small so one lucky split does not decide the winner.

sections.heading: Trends and factors that affect results
sections.body:
The exam asks you to identify trends and factors that could affect results. Common culprits:

- **Data leakage**: test examples (or near-duplicates) also appear in training data, which inflates scores. Dedup across splits.
- **Distribution shift**: production inputs differ from the evaluation set (new topics, languages, lengths).
- **Class imbalance**: high accuracy that just reflects the majority class; check per-class precision and recall.
- **Confounders and aggregation**: a trend in aggregated data can reverse inside subgroups (Simpson's paradox), so slice results by key segments.
- **Outliers**: a few extreme values can dominate means and MSE; check medians and plots.
- **Small samples**: differences within noise; repeat runs or use confidence intervals.

Correlation in a chart is not causation. Treat a trend as a hypothesis to test, not a conclusion.

keyPoints: Histogram for distributions, scatter for relationships, line for change over time, bar for categories.
Training loss falling while validation loss rises signals overfitting.
R² can be negative; explained variance ignores constant bias in residuals.
Check for leakage, shift, imbalance and confounders before trusting a metric.

gotchas.trap: R² and explained variance are always identical.
gotchas.correct: They match only when residuals have zero mean. A biased model can have high explained variance but lower R².

gotchas.trap: A lower training loss means the model is better.
gotchas.correct: Only validation or test performance on unseen data tells you whether it generalises.

gotchas.trap: 95% accuracy proves the classifier works.
gotchas.correct: With imbalanced classes this can be the majority-class rate. Check per-class metrics.

lessons.lab: Train two small regression models on the same dataset. Plot their predictions against true values as scatter plots, compute R² and explained variance for each, then add a constant +5 to one model's predictions and recompute. Note which metric changes and explain why.

lessons.title: Embeddings and vector databases for RAG data
lessons.summary: Turning curated content into searchable vectors: choosing an embedding model, chunking, similarity search, vector databases and reranking.

sections.heading: From text to vectors
sections.body:
An **embedding model** maps text to a dense vector so that semantically similar texts land close together. Official NCA-GENL subtopics include "curate and embed content datasets for RAG" and "select and use models to create text embeddings".

NVIDIA ships embedding and reranking models as **NeMo Retriever** microservices within **NIM** (text embedding and text reranking). Rules that matter regardless of model:

- **Use the same embedding model** for documents and queries. Vectors from different models live in different spaces and cannot be compared.
- **Re-embed the whole corpus** if you change the embedding model.
- Stay within the model's **input length limit**, which is counted in tokens.

sections.heading: Chunking and metadata
sections.body:
Documents are split into **chunks** before embedding.

- Chunks that are too large blur several topics into one vector and waste context in the prompt.
- Chunks that are too small lose the surrounding meaning.
- A small **overlap** between chunks keeps sentences that span a boundary retrievable.

Store **metadata** with each chunk (source, date, section, access level). That enables filtering ("only 2025 policies") and citations in answers. Curate before you embed: dedup and remove boilerplate, or retrieval will return the same passage many times.

sections.heading: Vector databases and retrieval
sections.body:
A **vector database** (the exam reading list names **Milvus**) stores embeddings and runs **approximate nearest-neighbour (ANN)** search, usually by cosine similarity or inner product. ANN indexes trade a little recall for much lower latency than brute-force comparison over millions of vectors.

A typical RAG retrieval flow:

1. Embed the user query with the same model used for documents.
2. Retrieve the top-k nearest chunks, optionally with metadata filters.
3. **Rerank** the candidates with a reranking model, which scores each query–chunk pair more precisely.
4. Pass the best chunks to the LLM as context.

Retrieval-augmented generation grounds answers in your current, private data without retraining the LLM, and lets the answer cite its sources.

keyPoints: Embed queries and documents with the same model; re-embed everything if you switch models.
Chunk size and overlap trade off precision against context.
Vector databases do approximate nearest-neighbour search; Milvus is on the reading list.
NeMo Retriever NIMs provide NVIDIA embedding and reranking models.
Rerank top-k candidates for higher precision before generation.

gotchas.trap: You can switch embedding models and keep the existing index.
gotchas.correct: Vectors from different models are not comparable. Re-embed the corpus with the new model.

gotchas.trap: RAG requires fine-tuning the LLM on your documents.
gotchas.correct: RAG retrieves relevant content at query time and adds it to the prompt; no retraining is needed.

lessons.lab: Embed 50 FAQ answers with one embedding model, then embed five user questions and retrieve the top 3 answers by cosine similarity. Repeat with chunks half the size and compare whether the correct answer still ranks first.

lessons.title: Designing LLM experiments
lessons.summary: How to set up an experiment you can trust: a baseline, clean train/validation/test splits, a sensible hyperparameter search and tracked, reproducible runs.

sections.heading: Start with a baseline
sections.body:
An experiment answers one question: *did this change make the model better than what we had?* You can only answer that with a **baseline**.

- For an LLM application, the usual baseline is the **base or instruction-tuned model with a simple zero-shot or few-shot prompt**. Fine-tuning or RAG must beat it on the same evaluation set to justify the cost.
- For a classic ML task, a trivial baseline (always predict the majority class) shows whether the model learned anything at all.
- **Change one thing at a time.** If you swap the model, the prompt and the data together, you cannot tell which change caused the result.

The NCA-GENL exam page lists "run experiments that evaluate models and pipelines" and "evaluate, refine and benchmark models" as Experimentation subtopics, so expect questions on how to set up a fair comparison.

sections.heading: Train, validation and test splits
sections.body:
| Split | Used for | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| **Training** | Updating model weights | The model sees it every epoch |
| **Validation (dev)** | Choosing hyperparameters, early stopping, comparing prompts | You look at it many times |
| **Test (held-out)** | Final, unbiased estimate | Touch it once, at the end |

Common mistakes:

- **Tuning on the test set.** Every time you pick a setting because it scored best on test data, the test score becomes optimistic.
- **Leakage.** Near-duplicate documents in both training and test data, or features that encode the label, inflate scores. Deduplicate before splitting (NeMo Curator offers exact, fuzzy and semantic deduplication).
- **Benchmark contamination.** Public benchmark questions can appear in web-scale pretraining data, so a high score may reflect memorisation. Decontaminate training data against your evaluation sets.
- **Wrong split shape.** For imbalanced labels, use a **stratified** split. For time-dependent data, split by time so the model never trains on the future.

When data is small, **k-fold cross-validation** gives a steadier estimate than one split. Cross-validation is named on the exam page under ML fundamentals.

sections.heading: Hyperparameters that matter
sections.body:
For fine-tuning LLMs, the settings that most often decide success are:

- **Learning rate.** Too high and loss spikes or diverges, and the model can forget general skills. Too low and training barely moves. Usually the first thing to tune.
- **Epochs / steps.** Too many on a small dataset overfits. Use **early stopping** on validation loss.
- **Batch size** (and gradient accumulation). It affects stability and memory.
- **PEFT settings.** For LoRA, the rank *r* and scaling *alpha* control how many trainable parameters the adapter has.
- **Decoding settings at evaluation time.** Temperature, top-k and top-p change the outputs you score, so fix them (often temperature 0 or greedy) when comparing models.

Search strategies: grid search tries every combination; **random search** usually finds good settings with fewer runs when only a few hyperparameters matter. Always pick the winner on the **validation** set.

sections.heading: Track every run
sections.body:
A run you cannot reproduce is not evidence. For each run record:

- code version, dataset version and split, and the base model checkpoint
- every hyperparameter and the **random seed**
- training and validation curves, final metrics, and sample outputs
- hardware and software versions

Experiment trackers such as Weights & Biases (its quickstart is on the official NCA-GENL reading list) log these automatically and let you compare runs side by side. Run several seeds when differences are small. A one-point gain from a single run may just be noise.

keyPoints: Every experiment needs a baseline; for LLM apps that is usually the base model with a simple prompt.
Tune on validation data; use the test set once for the final number.
Deduplicate before splitting and decontaminate training data against evaluation sets.
Learning rate and number of epochs are the hyperparameters most likely to break fine-tuning.
Log code, data, config, seed and metrics for every run so results are reproducible.

gotchas.trap: Reporting the test score of the configuration that scored best on the test set.
gotchas.correct: Select on the validation set, then report test once. Selecting on test makes the test score optimistic.

gotchas.trap: Changing the model, prompt and data in the same experiment.
gotchas.correct: Change one variable at a time against a fixed baseline so you know what caused the difference.

gotchas.trap: Treating a small gain from one run as a real improvement.
gotchas.correct: Repeat with several seeds or compute confidence intervals before claiming a win.

lessons.lab: Pick a small classification dataset. Build a majority-class baseline, then a zero-shot LLM prompt baseline, then a few-shot prompt. Use a stratified train/validation/test split, choose the best prompt on validation only, and report test accuracy and F1 once. Log every run with its prompt, seed and metrics.

lessons.title: Automatic metrics and benchmarks
lessons.summary: What perplexity, BLEU, ROUGE, accuracy, precision, recall and F1 actually measure, when each is misleading, and how to read benchmark results.

sections.heading: Perplexity
sections.body:
**Perplexity** measures how well a language model predicts held-out text. It is the exponential of the average negative log-likelihood per token, so **lower is better**.

- It is useful for tracking pretraining or domain-adaptation progress on held-out data.
- It does **not** measure whether answers are correct, helpful or safe.
- Perplexities from models with **different tokenizers** are not directly comparable, because "per token" means different things.

sections.heading: Overlap metrics: BLEU and ROUGE
sections.body:
Both compare generated text with one or more **reference** texts by counting overlapping n-grams.

| Metric | Orientation | Typical task |
|---|---|---|
| **BLEU** | Precision of n-grams, with a brevity penalty for short outputs | Machine translation |
| **ROUGE** | Recall-oriented (ROUGE-N for n-grams, ROUGE-L for longest common subsequence) | Summarisation |

Limits: they reward wording, not meaning. A correct paraphrase can score low, and a fluent answer with a wrong fact can score high. Embedding-based metrics such as **BERTScore** compare meaning with contextual embeddings and correlate better with human judgement on many tasks. For open-ended chat, overlap metrics are a poor fit.

sections.heading: Classification metrics
sections.body:
When the LLM output is a label (sentiment, intent, a yes/no answer), use classification metrics from the scikit-learn metrics guide on the official reading list:

- **Accuracy** = correct / total. Misleading with **class imbalance**: 98% accuracy on data that is 98% negative may mean the model never finds a positive.
- **Precision** = TP / (TP + FP). How many flagged items were right. Prioritise it when false alarms are costly.
- **Recall** = TP / (TP + FN). How many real positives were found. Prioritise it when misses are costly (fraud, safety).
- **F1** = harmonic mean of precision and recall. A single score that punishes a model that sacrifices one for the other.
- **Exact match** is common for short-answer QA.

For regression-style outputs, the Data Analysis domain covers loss functions and explained variance.

sections.heading: Benchmarks and harnesses
sections.body:
Public benchmarks give a standard yardstick:

- **MMLU**: multiple-choice questions across 57 subjects, testing broad knowledge.
- **TruthfulQA**: tests whether a model repeats common misconceptions.
- **HELM**: a framework that reports many metrics (accuracy, calibration, robustness, fairness, toxicity, efficiency) across many scenarios, not one number.

Tools such as EleutherAI's **lm-evaluation-harness** (official reading) run many benchmarks with the same prompts and settings, which makes comparisons fair. NVIDIA's **NeMo Evaluator** (a NeMo Framework library and NeMo Helix service) covers academic benchmarks, LLM-as-judge, RAG and agentic evaluation.

Cautions: benchmark scores can be **contaminated** by training data; prompt format and few-shot count change scores; and a general benchmark rarely predicts performance on *your* task. Always add a task-specific evaluation set.

keyPoints: Perplexity: lower is better, measures prediction of text, not answer quality; compare only with the same tokenizer.
BLEU is precision-oriented (translation); ROUGE is recall-oriented (summarisation); both reward wording, not meaning.
Use precision when false positives are costly, recall when misses are costly, F1 to balance them.
Accuracy misleads on imbalanced data.
Benchmarks need identical prompts and settings, and can be contaminated; add a task-specific test set.

gotchas.trap: Using perplexity to prove a chatbot gives correct answers.
gotchas.correct: Perplexity measures how well the model predicts text. Use task metrics, human review or LLM-as-judge for answer quality.

gotchas.trap: Comparing perplexity between models with different tokenizers.
gotchas.correct: Per-token perplexity depends on the vocabulary, so compare only models that share a tokenizer, or normalise differently.

gotchas.trap: Choosing a model on MMLU alone for a domain-specific support bot.
gotchas.correct: General benchmarks are a screen. Build an evaluation set from your own task.

lessons.lab: Install lm-evaluation-harness and score two small open models on one multiple-choice task with identical settings. Then score the same models on 50 of your own labelled examples with accuracy and F1, and compare the rankings.

lessons.title: Human, LLM-as-judge and RAG evaluation
lessons.summary: How to evaluate open-ended output with human raters and LLM judges, the known biases of LLM judges, and the separate metrics for the retrieval and generation halves of a RAG pipeline.

sections.heading: Human evaluation
sections.body:
Humans remain the reference for helpfulness, tone and harm. Make human evaluation reliable:

- Write a **rubric** with clear criteria and examples for each score.
- Prefer **pairwise comparison** (A vs B) over absolute 1-10 scores; people agree more on which is better.
- **Blind** raters to which model produced which output, and randomise order.
- Measure **inter-annotator agreement**; low agreement means the rubric is unclear.

Human evaluation is slow and expensive, so teams use it to calibrate cheaper automatic methods.

sections.heading: LLM-as-a-judge
sections.body:
A strong LLM grades outputs against a rubric or picks the better of two answers. The MT-Bench study found strong LLM judges can agree with human preferences about as often as humans agree with each other, which makes them a scalable proxy.

Known biases and mitigations:

| Bias | What happens | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| **Position bias** | Prefers the first (or second) answer | Run both orders; count a win only if it holds when swapped |
| **Verbosity bias** | Prefers longer answers | Rubric that rewards concision; length controls |
| **Self-enhancement bias** | Prefers outputs from its own model family | Use a different judge model, or several |
| **Limited reasoning** | Misgrades maths or code | Give a reference answer; ask the judge to reason first |

Validate the judge against a sample of human labels before trusting it. NVIDIA's NeMo Evaluator (a NeMo Framework library, also offered as a service in NeMo Helix, the recently introduced successor to the archived NeMo microservices) supports LLM-as-judge evaluation. Product names here have changed recently, so focus on the concept.

sections.heading: Evaluating RAG: two halves
sections.body:
A RAG answer can fail because retrieval found the wrong passages, or because the generator ignored or contradicted good passages. Measure each half.

**Retrieval metrics** (need relevance labels):

- **Recall@k**: share of the relevant documents that appear in the top *k*. If it is low, the generator never sees the evidence.
- **Precision@k**: share of the top *k* that are relevant. Low precision floods the context with noise.
- **MRR** (mean reciprocal rank) and **nDCG**: reward putting relevant documents near the top.

**Generation metrics** (RAGAS-style, often scored by an LLM judge):

- **Faithfulness / groundedness**: are the answer's claims supported by the retrieved context? Low faithfulness is hallucination.
- **Answer relevance**: does the answer address the question?
- **Context relevance**: is the retrieved context focused on the question?

Diagnosis: low recall@k → fix chunking, embeddings, hybrid search or add a reranker. High recall but low faithfulness → fix the prompt ("answer only from the context"), the model, or the context order.

keyPoints: Pairwise, blinded, rubric-based human evaluation with measured inter-annotator agreement is the most reliable form.
LLM judges have position, verbosity and self-enhancement biases; swap orders and validate against human labels.
Evaluate RAG retrieval (recall@k, precision@k, MRR, nDCG) separately from generation (faithfulness, answer relevance).
Low recall@k means the evidence never reached the model; low faithfulness with good recall means the generator is the problem.

gotchas.trap: Using one LLM-judge pass with answer A always shown first.
gotchas.correct: Evaluate both orders to cancel position bias.

gotchas.trap: Fine-tuning the generator when retrieval recall is low.
gotchas.correct: If the right passage is not retrieved, fix retrieval first: chunking, embeddings, hybrid search or reranking.

gotchas.trap: Assuming the judge model is accurate because it is large.
gotchas.correct: Check the judge against a human-labelled sample before relying on it.

lessons.lab: Take 30 questions with known source passages. Measure recall@5 of your retriever. Then have an LLM judge score faithfulness of the generated answers, run each pairwise comparison in both orders, and compare 10 judge verdicts with your own.

lessons.title: Prompting vs RAG vs fine-tuning, and diagnosing failures
lessons.summary: A decision framework for prompting, RAG, PEFT and full fine-tuning, plus how to recognise and fix hallucination, overfitting, underfitting and catastrophic forgetting.

sections.heading: Pick the lightest method that works
sections.body:
| Approach | Changes weights? | Best for | Costs |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Prompt engineering** (zero/few-shot, chain-of-thought) | No | Fast iteration, format and task instructions | Longer prompts at inference |
| **RAG** | No | Fresh, private or fast-changing knowledge; citations | Retrieval infrastructure, latency |
| **Prompt tuning / p-tuning** | Learns soft prompt embeddings; base frozen | Task adaptation with very few trainable parameters | Needs training data |
| **PEFT (LoRA)** | Small adapter matrices; base frozen | Style, format, domain behaviour, specialised tasks | Training run, labelled data |
| **Full fine-tuning** | All weights | Large shifts with lots of data | Most compute; highest forgetting risk |

A common rule of thumb: **RAG adds knowledge, fine-tuning changes behaviour.** Start with prompting, add RAG when the model lacks facts, and fine-tune when it needs a consistent style, format or skill that prompts cannot deliver. Methods combine: a LoRA-tuned model can sit behind a RAG pipeline.

sections.heading: Hallucination
sections.body:
A hallucination is fluent output that is not supported by the input or by facts.

Causes: missing knowledge (the fact postdates training or is private), weak retrieval, prompts that pressure the model to always answer, and high-temperature sampling.

Fixes:

- **Ground with RAG** and instruct the model to answer only from the provided context and say when it does not know.
- Ask for **citations** so claims can be checked.
- Lower the temperature for factual tasks.
- Measure **faithfulness** in evaluation and add guardrails (NeMo Guardrails has retrieval and output rails) for production.

Fine-tuning on new facts is a weak fix: it is costly to repeat each time facts change and does not reliably stop invented answers.

sections.heading: Overfitting and underfitting
sections.body:
Read the loss curves:

| Pattern | Diagnosis | Fixes |
|---|---|---|
| Training loss falls, **validation loss rises** | **Overfitting** (memorising) | Early stopping, fewer epochs, more or more varied data, regularisation (dropout, weight decay), data augmentation, smaller LoRA rank |
| **Both stay high** | **Underfitting** | Train longer, raise learning rate carefully, larger model or rank, better features or data |
| Loss spikes or becomes NaN | Unstable training | Lower learning rate, warm-up, gradient clipping, check data |

The NVIDIA DLI Fundamentals of Deep Learning course (on the exam page) covers the bias-variance trade-off and overfitting with data augmentation and transfer learning.

sections.heading: Catastrophic forgetting
sections.body:
**Catastrophic forgetting** is when fine-tuning on a narrow new task overwrites what the model knew, so general skills (or earlier tasks) degrade.

Symptoms: the tuned model does its new task well, but scores drop on general benchmarks or it loses instruction-following or safety behaviour.

Mitigations:

- **PEFT** such as LoRA or p-tuning keeps base weights frozen, so the original model is intact and the adapter can be removed.
- **Mix in general data** (replay) alongside task data.
- Use a **lower learning rate** and fewer epochs.
- Regularisation methods such as elastic weight consolidation (EWC) penalise changes to weights important for earlier tasks.
- **Always re-run general benchmarks** after fine-tuning, not only the task metric.

keyPoints: Prompt first, RAG for knowledge, fine-tune for behaviour; methods can be combined.
RAG is the main fix for hallucination about fresh or private facts; ask for citations and measure faithfulness.
Training loss down + validation loss up = overfitting; both high = underfitting.
Catastrophic forgetting: narrow fine-tuning erodes general ability; PEFT, data mixing and lower learning rates reduce it.
After any fine-tune, re-evaluate on general benchmarks as well as the target task.

gotchas.trap: Fine-tuning a model every week to teach it this week's policy changes.
gotchas.correct: Put changing knowledge in a RAG index; update the documents, not the weights.

gotchas.trap: Fixing overfitting by training for more epochs.
gotchas.correct: More epochs make overfitting worse. Use early stopping, more data or regularisation.

gotchas.trap: Judging a fine-tune only on the target task.
gotchas.correct: Also measure general benchmarks to catch catastrophic forgetting.

lessons.lab: Fine-tune a small model with LoRA on a narrow dataset for several epochs. Plot training and validation loss, mark where early stopping would trigger, and compare a general benchmark score before and after tuning to look for forgetting.

lessons.title: RLHF data, technology evaluation and performance testing
lessons.summary: The remaining official Experimentation subtopics: collecting human preference data for RLHF, preparing datasets, judging technologies on cost, portability, compatibility and usability, and load-testing LLM applications.

sections.heading: Human data for RLHF
sections.body:
The exam page lists "understand or take part in collecting human data for RLHF". In the InstructGPT recipe:

1. **Supervised fine-tuning (SFT)** on human-written demonstrations.
2. **Preference collection**: annotators see several model outputs for a prompt and **rank or compare** them.
3. A **reward model** is trained to predict those preferences.
4. The policy is optimised against the reward model with reinforcement learning (PPO), with a penalty that keeps it close to the SFT model.

Good preference data needs clear labelling guidelines, diverse and trained annotators, quality checks such as agreement on overlap items, and separate criteria where needed (Llama 2, for example, collected helpfulness and safety preferences separately). Annotators' consent and privacy matter too (see Trustworthy AI).

sections.heading: Preparing large datasets
sections.body:
Pretraining, fine-tuning and RLHF all start with data work (an official subtopic):

- **Collect / scrape** text, respecting licences and robots rules.
- **Clean and filter**: language ID, heuristic quality filters, classifier-based quality and safety filters.
- **Deduplicate**: exact, fuzzy (MinHash + LSH) and semantic deduplication; NeMo Curator does all three on GPUs.
- **Tokenize** with the model's own tokenizer and check sequence lengths against the context window.
- **Decontaminate** against evaluation sets so test scores stay honest.

sections.heading: Evaluating technologies
sections.body:
The exam asks you to evaluate technologies on four axes:

- **Cost**: GPU hours to train, cost per token or per request to serve, engineering time.
- **Portability**: can the model or service move between clouds, data centres and workstations? Containers (NIM runs as a container from NGC) and exchange formats such as ONNX help.
- **Compatibility**: does it fit your hardware, frameworks and APIs? For example, NIM LLM microservices expose an OpenAI-compatible API, so existing client code can switch with little change.
- **Usability**: documentation, tooling and how hard it is for the team to operate.

Score candidates on the same task-specific evaluation set and the same load test, not on vendor claims.

sections.heading: Hardware and software tests for LLM apps
sections.body:
Quality is not enough; an LLM app also has to be fast and stable. Key measurements:

- **Time to first token (TTFT)**: how long until streaming starts. Dominates perceived responsiveness in chat.
- **Inter-token latency** and total latency.
- **Throughput**: tokens or requests per second across all users.
- Behaviour under realistic **concurrency** and prompt/response lengths.

Batching (such as dynamic batching in NVIDIA Dynamo-Triton, formerly Triton Inference Server) raises GPU utilisation and throughput but can add latency per request, so test at the concurrency you expect in production. NIM documentation includes an LLM benchmarking guide, and Dynamo-Triton exposes GPU utilisation, throughput and latency metrics for Prometheus.

keyPoints: RLHF: SFT, then human rankings of outputs, then a reward model, then RL (PPO) against it.
Data prep: filter, deduplicate, tokenize and decontaminate before training.
Evaluate technologies on cost, portability, compatibility and usability using your own workload.
Load-test with realistic concurrency; report TTFT, latency and throughput together.

gotchas.trap: Asking annotators to give each response an absolute score with no guidelines.
gotchas.correct: Use clear guidelines and pairwise or ranked comparisons, and check agreement.

gotchas.trap: Benchmarking an LLM service with one request at a time and calling the latency the production figure.
gotchas.correct: Measure under expected concurrency and request lengths; batching changes the latency/throughput trade-off.

lessons.lab: Run an LLM endpoint (a NIM container or another server) and send requests at concurrency 1, 8 and 32. Record TTFT, total latency and tokens per second at each level, and explain the trade-off you see.

lessons.title: Python toolkit for LLM applications
lessons.summary: Know what NumPy, pandas, PyTorch, Hugging Face Transformers, spaCy and orchestration frameworks such as LangChain or LlamaIndex each do in an LLM app, and how NVIDIA GPU libraries speed them up.

sections.heading: Arrays and tables: NumPy and pandas
sections.body:
- **NumPy** gives you n-dimensional arrays and vectorised maths. Embeddings are just float arrays, so cosine similarity, normalisation and batching are NumPy one-liners. Prefer vectorised operations over Python loops.
- **pandas** gives you labelled DataFrames for loading, cleaning, joining and summarising tabular data (CSV logs, evaluation results, chunk metadata).
- On a GPU, **cuDF** offers a pandas-like DataFrame, and **`cudf.pandas`** accelerates existing pandas code with zero code changes (`%load_ext cudf.pandas` in Jupyter, or `python -m cudf.pandas script.py`). Unsupported operations fall back to pandas on the CPU.
- **cuML** mirrors the scikit-learn `fit` / `predict` / `transform` API on the GPU for traditional ML.

sections.heading: Deep learning: PyTorch
sections.body:
PyTorch is the framework used in NVIDIA's Fundamentals of Deep Learning course, and NVIDIA's LLM libraries (Megatron Bridge, TensorRT-LLM) are now PyTorch-native.
- **Tensors** are GPU-capable arrays. Move the model *and* its inputs to the same device (`model.to(device)`, `x.to(device)`), or PyTorch raises a device-mismatch error.
- A training step is: forward pass, loss, `loss.backward()`, `optimizer.step()`, `optimizer.zero_grad()`.
- For inference, switch to evaluation mode and disable gradient tracking to save memory.

sections.heading: Models and text: Hugging Face Transformers and spaCy
sections.body:
- **Transformers** loads pretrained checkpoints with a matching **tokenizer**. Always use the tokenizer that ships with the checkpoint: a different vocabulary produces meaningless token IDs.
- High-level **pipelines** wrap tokenise → model → decode for tasks such as summarisation or text generation. They are good for prototyping, not for high-throughput serving.
- **spaCy** (on the official reading list) handles classic NLP: tokenisation, sentence splitting, part-of-speech tags and named-entity recognition. It is useful for cleaning text and splitting documents before chunking.

sections.heading: Orchestration: LangChain and LlamaIndex style frameworks
sections.body:
These frameworks glue the pieces of an LLM app together. They do not train or serve models.
- **Loaders and splitters** read documents and chunk them.
- **Embeddings and vector stores** index the chunks.
- **Retrievers** fetch the top-k relevant chunks for a query.
- **Chains, query engines or agents** build the prompt, call the LLM and post-process the answer.

Because NIM exposes an OpenAI-compatible API, these frameworks can point at a self-hosted NIM endpoint the same way they point at a hosted API. NVIDIA's GenerativeAIExamples repository has reference RAG apps built this way.

keyPoints: NumPy = arrays and vectorised maths; pandas = labelled tables; cuDF / cudf.pandas = the same on a GPU.
cuML follows the scikit-learn API for GPU-accelerated traditional ML.
PyTorch: the model and its inputs must be on the same device.
Use the tokenizer that matches the model checkpoint.
LangChain / LlamaIndex orchestrate load → chunk → embed → retrieve → prompt → generate. They do not serve models.

gotchas.trap: cudf.pandas fails on any operation the GPU does not support.
gotchas.correct: It falls back to pandas on the CPU for unsupported operations.

gotchas.trap: LangChain is an inference server that makes the model faster.
gotchas.correct: It is an orchestration framework. Speed comes from the serving stack (NIM, TensorRT-LLM, Dynamo-Triton).

gotchas.trap: Any tokenizer works with any model as long as the language matches.
gotchas.correct: Token IDs are vocabulary-specific. Load the tokenizer from the same checkpoint as the model.

lessons.lab: In a notebook, load a CSV of support tickets with pandas, then rerun the same cells after `%load_ext cudf.pandas` and compare timings. Next, embed 20 ticket texts with any embedding model and use NumPy to find the three nearest neighbours of a new query by cosine similarity.

lessons.title: The NVIDIA generative AI software stack
lessons.summary: Map each NVIDIA product to its job: NGC for software, NeMo for building and customising models, NIM for packaged inference, Dynamo-Triton for multi-framework serving, TensorRT-LLM and TensorRT for optimisation.

sections.heading: NGC: where the software comes from
sections.body:
NGC is "a curated set of GPU-optimized software for AI, HPC, and Visualization". It hosts **containers, pretrained models, Helm charts and SDKs**.
- The container registry is **nvcr.io**.
- `docker login nvcr.io` uses the literal username **`$oauthtoken`** and an **NGC API key** as the password.
- Use personal or service keys. The legacy API key type is being retired.

Pulling an NGC framework container gives you a tested combination of CUDA, libraries and framework versions instead of building your own.

sections.heading: NeMo: build and customise models
sections.body:
The NeMo Framework has been restructured into modular libraries. For LLMs, the current training library is **NeMo Megatron Bridge**, "a PyTorch-native library within the NeMo Framework" built on Megatron Core. It covers:
- pretraining, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and PEFT (LoRA, DoRA)
- **Hugging Face ↔ Megatron checkpoint conversion**
- tensor, pipeline, context and expert parallelism, with BF16, FP8 and FP4 mixed precision.

Related libraries include **NeMo Curator** (data curation), **NeMo Evaluator**, NeMo RL and NeMo Export-Deploy. **NeMo Guardrails** adds programmable input, dialog, retrieval, execution and output rails to an app.

Older material calls the stack "NeMo 2.0", "NeMo Megatron" or NeMo Launcher. Treat those as history, and learn the concepts rather than exact library names.

sections.heading: NIM: packaged inference microservices
sections.body:
NVIDIA NIM microservices are for "accelerating the deployment of foundation models on any cloud or data center". A NIM is a container from NGC with an optimised runtime.
- LLM NIMs expose an **OpenAI-compatible API**.
- They use **TensorRT-LLM, vLLM or SGLang** backends with optimised profiles for the detected GPU.
- Other categories include vision-language models, **NeMo Retriever** (embedding, reranking), speech and NemoGuard safety models.
- You can try them at build.nvidia.com (the API catalog). Production use is licensed through NVIDIA AI Enterprise, and the Developer Program allows free development use.
- On Kubernetes, the **NIM Operator** manages NIM deployments.

sections.heading: Dynamo-Triton, TensorRT-LLM and TensorRT
sections.body:
| Product | Job |
|---|---|
| **Dynamo-Triton (formerly Triton Inference Server)** | Open-source server for many frameworks (TensorRT, TensorRT-LLM, PyTorch, ONNX Runtime, Python, vLLM and more) with a model repository, dynamic batching, concurrent model execution and HTTP/gRPC APIs |
| **NVIDIA Dynamo** | A separate, LLM-focused distributed inference framework (disaggregated prefill/decode serving, prefix caching, KV-cache offload) |
| **TensorRT-LLM** | Open-source, PyTorch-native LLM inference library: in-flight batching, paged KV cache, quantisation (FP8, FP4), speculative decoding and parallelism |
| **TensorRT** | SDK that optimises trained networks, often imported from **ONNX**, into fast inference engines |

Rule of thumb: NIM if you want an LLM endpoint with the least effort; Dynamo-Triton if you serve many model types; TensorRT-LLM if you are tuning the LLM engine itself.

keyPoints: NGC = GPU-optimised containers, models and Helm charts on nvcr.io (log in as $oauthtoken with an API key).
NeMo Megatron Bridge = current PyTorch-native LLM training and PEFT library, with HF ↔ Megatron conversion.
NIM = containerised, optimised inference with an OpenAI-compatible API (TensorRT-LLM, vLLM or SGLang backends).
Dynamo-Triton (formerly Triton Inference Server) = multi-framework serving with dynamic batching.
TensorRT-LLM = LLM engine optimisation; TensorRT + ONNX = general model optimisation.

gotchas.trap: NVIDIA Dynamo is just the new name for Triton.
gotchas.correct: Triton was renamed Dynamo-Triton. Dynamo itself is a separate LLM-focused distributed inference framework.

gotchas.trap: NIM is a training framework.
gotchas.correct: NIM packages models for inference. Training and fine-tuning belong to NeMo libraries such as Megatron Bridge.

gotchas.trap: Log in to nvcr.io with your NVIDIA account email and password.
gotchas.correct: Use the username $oauthtoken and an NGC API key as the password.

Then write a one-page table mapping five tasks (clean a corpus, fine-tune with LoRA, serve an ONNX vision model, serve an LLM chatbot, block PII in answers) to the NVIDIA product you would use.
